title: Seeing it is seeing
hook: whoever sees dependent origination sees the dhamma (MN 28)

segments.voice: Yesterday: where the chain breaks, and your line, cut between. Did you feel a first arrow, and skip the second, even once? Day three hundred fifty-one.

A monk named Vakkali loved the Buddha so much that he couldn't stop looking at him. He followed him around just to see his face. Years later, when Vakkali was gravely ill, the Buddha came to his bedside, and Vakkali tried to get up. He said that for a long time he'd wanted to come and see the Blessed One, but his body hadn't let him. The Buddha's answer is one of the most quoted lines in the canon, and it changes what seeing means. Today, we come back to the elephant's footprint, where this block began.
screen: `VAKKALI COULDN'T STOP LOOKING.` → `A BEDSIDE VISIT.` → `WHAT SEEING MEANS.`

segments.voice: Here's what the Buddha told Vakkali, in the Connected Discourses. Enough, Vakkali. Why do you want to see this rotting body? Whoever sees the Dhamma sees me; whoever sees me sees the Dhamma. It isn't cold. It's a gift: you don't need my face; you need what I've been pointing at. Now go back to the very first day of this block, the elephant's footprint, Sariputta's great talk in the Middle-Length Discourses. Near its end, after walking through the body's elements and the five heaps, Sariputta quotes the Buddha with a line that has the same shape. Whoever sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma. Whoever sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination. Put the two together and something comes into focus. To see the Buddha is to see the Dhamma. To see the Dhamma is to see dependent arising: this, because of that. So the deepest seeing in Buddhism isn't of a person or a place or a vision. It's seeing how things lean on each other. How a mood leans on sleep. How craving leans on feeling. How dukkha leans on craving, and ends when craving ends. Sariputta draws the conclusion right there in the sutta: the five heaps are dependently arisen, and the desire and clinging for them is the origin of dukkha. Seeing it isn't a step before the real thing. The seeing is the real thing. That's why the title repeats itself: seeing it is seeing.
screen: `WHOEVER SEES THE DHAMMA SEES ME.` · `BACK TO THE ELEPHANT'S FOOTPRINT.` · `TO SEE DEPENDENT ARISING.` · `THE SEEING IS THE REAL THING.` · then, large: `SEEING IT IS SEEING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to see one connection clearly. Sit and breathe. Choose one small thing happening in you right now: a sound you hear, an ache, a thought. Ask what it depends on. The sound depends on the ear, the air, the source. The ache depends on how you're sitting. Stay with just one link until you can see it plainly, without commentary. Then rest, and let the seeing be enough. The bell holds the time.
Seeing it is seeing. Whoever sees dependent arising sees the Dhamma, and whoever sees the Dhamma sees the Buddha.
Your line: seeing it is seeing. Today, when you understand why something happened, pause and notice that the understanding itself is a kind of seeing. Day three hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often pair the line from MN 28 with the Buddha's words to Vakkali to explain that the teaching, not the teacher's body, is what students are meant to see.

match.prompt: match each line to who said or heard it.
pairs: wanted to see the Buddha's body

myth: the Buddha told Vakkali to keep gazing at him
he said: why see this body? whoever sees the Dhamma sees me.
MN 28, the elephant's footprint, contains the line about dependent origination
Sariputta quotes it near the end of the talk.
in Buddhism, seeing the Dhamma means having a vision of light
it means seeing dependent arising: how things lean on each other.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha, at the bedside of a sick monk who has always longed to look at you. he tries to get up to see you. what do you say?
options: stay and look at me as long as you like.
why see this body? whoever sees the Dhamma sees me.
you must get well before you see me.
fork.reveal: the Buddha turned Vakkali's eyes from his body to the teaching: whoever sees the Dhamma sees me.

original.note: Pali dhamma, Sanskrit dharma: the teaching, and the way things are, which the teaching points to.

trapdoor: what you thought: seeing the Dhamma is a mystical vision.
what it means: it's seeing how things arise from conditions, and how dukkha ends when its conditions end.
what a scholar hears: MN 28 has Sariputta cite yo paṭiccasamuppādaṃ passati so dhammaṃ passati, and SN 22.87 has yo kho dhammaṃ passati so maṃ passati; both make seeing the teaching the true meeting.

sources.ref: MN 28 (Mahahatthipadopama Sutta), the line on dependent origination

notes: SN 22.87 paraphrased (spoken without quotation marks): confirm 'Enough, Vakkali, why see this foul/putrid body? Whoever sees the Dhamma sees me; whoever sees me sees the Dhamma.'
Vakkali's habit of gazing at the Buddha comes from the commentary and Theragatha tradition; the script says he 'loved the Buddha so much he couldn't stop looking': confirm or mark as tradition.
MN 28 conclusion paraphrased: the five aggregates affected by clinging are dependently arisen; desire, attachment etc. for them is the origin of dukkha. Confirm.
The Pali in the trapdoor should be checked.
